subtopic: TABLING OF REPORTS OF TARIFF BOARD

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TABLING OF REPORTS OF TARIFF BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to table copies, in English and in French, of four reports that have been submitted by the tariff board. The reports in question are as follows: reference No. 118, basic iron and steel products; reference No. 119, pipes and tubes of iron or steel; reference No. 121, waterproof footwear and rubber-soled canvas footwear; reference No. 122, zinc and zinc products. Three of the reports were submitted some time ago to my predecessor and were released by him for public distribution in June of this year. I am now tabling these reports and also transcripts of the evidence taken at the public hearings of the board, pursuant to section 6 of the Tariff Board Act. I am tabling also a report, and the transcript of evidence, relating to zinc and zinc products which was submitted to me by the chairman of the tariff board earlier this week.
I should like to comment briefly on each of these reports at this time and to indicate how the government proposes to deal with them. I hope my remarks will provide an answer to the question asked two days ago by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Schulz) and to similar questions which may be in the minds of other hon. members.
I wish to refer first to the reference relating to basic iron and steel products. In this very broad and important reference the board's inquiries related to some 113 existing tariff classifications. Of this total the board considered that 21 items were not in need of revision. It recommended that the remaining 92 items be reduced in number to 38. In detailed explanatory notes included in its report the board has furnished information which permits comparisons between the existing rates and the proposed rates of duty.
The effect of the board's recommendation is that some rates are increased while others are decreased. They are designed to provide what the tariff board considered, on the basis of the evidence presented to it, to be adequate protection where it is required.
With regard to the wording and arrangement of the proposed tariff items, the most striking change from the present situation is the substantial simplification of the iron and steel schedule accomplished by the elimination of numerous special purpose items, and the consolidation of the remaining items into four major groups relating to plate, structural, bars and sheet and strip respectively.
The tariff board's recommendations on pipes and tubes are also intended to bring up to date and simplify a section of the tariff which has become out of date. These recommendations, like those affecting basic iron and steel, involve reductions in some rates and increases in others. The board's terms of reference contemplated recommendations which would modernize the pipes and tubes schedule. The board's recommendations are, I believe, consistent with its terms of reference.
I wish to refer next to the report which has just been received, that on zinc and zinc products, as the situation with regard to these items is much like the situation with regard to the iron and steel items. In this reference the board was instructed to investigate and make recommendations regarding alleged anomalies in the existing tariff structure, having regard to the obligations and procedures of the general agreement on tariffs and trade. The board found that anomalies did exist, and it recommended changes to remove them. As in the case of the other reports to which I have referred, these changes involve some increases in rates of duty and also some decreases.
A review of the three reports to which I have referred leads to the conclusion that the proposed increases and decreases are broadly in balance, and that the recommendations taken together constitute what might be called a negotiable package. I would emphasize, however, that it is a package which requires negotiation with other countries and on which we could not, in view of existing international obligations, take unilateral action without giving other countries rights to withdraw concessions of value to Canadian exporters. The government is taking advantage of the present GATT negotiations in Geneva to undertake such negotiations.
I believe hon. members will be interested in some aspects of the negotiations. First, the

Tariff Board Reports
lists of the bound items which Canada is seeking to modify have been notified to other contracting parties and in some instances have been made public by them. There is no objection to this on our part. It does not necessarily follow, however, that the giving of notice of our desire to negotiate a particular item indicates an intention to raise the rate of duty thereon. Frequently the reverse will be the case, as when two or more existing classifications are to be combined under circumstances where the proposed new rate is lower than the average of the existing rates. In other instances what is involved may be merely a change in wording. I hope this will answer questions that have been asked and will also serve to clear up any possible misconceptions.
Second, the negotiations at Geneva will necessarily be conducted in private, and they will be conducted in so far as Canada is concerned with careful reference to the tariff board's recommendations. However, I should emphasize at this time that what ultimately emerges should be expected to differ in some respects from these recommendations. This will be the case not only because of the give and take that necessarily occurs in any such negotiations, but also because the government will wish in some instances to take account of the new developments affecting individual tariff items. After the negotiations are concluded, it would be the intention of the government to introduce in parliament at an appropriate time the tariff changes which the government considers to be desirable.
I would like to refer briefly to the fourth report which I am tabling today, namely that on waterproof footwear and rubber soled canvas footwear, reference No. 121. As hon. members will have noted, in making this reference to the tariff board my predecessor did not ask for recommendations. Accordingly none were made by the board in this report. However, on studying the report which is being tabled today I came to the conclusion that it might be useful to have the board prepare a supplementary report on this reference, including therein any recommendations which the board might deem warranted regarding the retention or modification of the present duties. This supplementary report has not yet been received; when it is it will be tabled in accordance with the provisions of the Tariff Board Act.

speechtext: These items may form the basis of agreement with other countries joining the Geneva convention on tariffs and trade. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TABLING OF REPORTS OF TARIFF BOARD
speechtext:
I think the hon. member is under a misapprehension, and may not have followed too closely the statement I gave to the house. The reports of the tariff board should not be regarded and should not be represented as reports the net effect of which is going to be increases in tariffs. The board has reviewed a great number of items in portions of the tariff which are very old and which the board found in many respects to be obsolete and, as I have indicated, what the board has recommended is a group of changes in the tariff in which there are as many decreases as increases.
These are bound items, that is to say bound against increase by our existing international obligations; and of course before the government can consider any submissions to parliament we have to negotiate with other countries to see where they stand on these matters. That is what will be carried out in the course of the next two months at Geneva and it will necessarily have to be in the light of those negotiations that the particular proposals which the government will be submitting to the house thereafter will be framed.

Mr. Speaker, with regard to the first question-has the government received any submission from any individual or group in respect of the Canadian rubber footwear companies since June 10, 1957,-the answer from June 21, 1957, is yes.
The second part of the question reads:
Will the government indicate if included in these representations are representations from any Canadian labour organizations, or from any corporations engaged in the fabrication of rubber footwear.

speechtext:

speechtext:
I wish to thank the hon. member for Westmorland for giving me notice of his question. This matter is covered by the Pension Act, and in each case is considered in the light of the provisions of the act. Section 45, subsection 1, of the Pension Act provides that when a pensioned widow remarries she is entitled to one year's pension as a final payment and her pension ceases.
Section 45, subsection 2, of the act makes the further provision that if the new husband dies within five years after such marriage and the widow is left in a dependent condition, her award may be restored by the *commission in whole or in part. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, October 24, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Monteith-Mr. Rea in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Old Age Security Act to increase the amount of monthly pension payable thereunder to fifty-five dollars per month, to reduce the basic residence requirements for pensioners from twenty years to ten years and to increase the length of permissible temporary absence of pensioners from Canada from three to six months.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have read with considerable interest the statement made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare in presenting to the house this particular resolution. I must apologize to him for not being here last night when he made his statement. I was engaged in constituency business, but had I known that my hon. friend was going to introduce the resolution I certainly would have made other arrangements.
Old Age Security Act
I am sure the house generally will find the resolution of great interest, and I am equally certain that the minister himself as he introduced it must have felt he was the pivot, as it were, in a rather historic effort by his party, because it represents the first time that anyone speaking for a Conservative government has put forward legislation having to do with some aspects of social welfare.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: That is not true; that is utterly untrue.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext:
It is not the first time, of course, that we in this house have dealt with matters in this field that have been proposed by spokesmen for the party represented by the government opposite, because hon. members will well recall, as we were reminded the other day by the former minister of agriculture, that in the election of 1930 the then leader of the Conservative party said to the people of Canada in substance, "Elect me; I will call parliament together and I will enact a real old age pensions measure." That statement was made in the town of Renfrew, in the town of Newcastle and in my own city of Windsor, and at a time when modifications in old age pensions would have been of great benefit to the people of this country.
The history of parliament between 1930 and 1935 will show that this promise of the then leader of the Conservative party, a distinguished gentleman who became prime minister, was not kept and his government did nothing whatsoever not only with regard to old age security or old age pensions but for that matter with regard to any particular measure relating to social welfare, except in its dying days when it brought in the unemployment insurance act which the Supreme Court of Canada shortly thereafter declared ultra vires.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: That statement is untrue.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: Take it quietly.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext:
My esteemed friend the Minister of National Health and Welfare was in the happy position last night, for which I sincerely congratulate him, of presenting to this house an amendment based upon an act of parliament introduced in 1951 by the government headed by the present Leader of the Opposition. In expressing our approval of this resolution and all its terms I might say, speaking for those of us on this side, that our approval can be understood particularly in the light of some of the facts which have preceded the introduction of this amendment from the time old age pensions were first enacted by this parliament.

Old Age Security Act
I think it is important to remember that in 1926 the minister of labour in the government of Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King proposed, on an enabling basis, legislation that would provide old age pensions to those citizens of Canada residing in provinces whose governments were prepared to accept the proposal made by the government of that day. It is a matter of history that the old age pensions proposal of that day would have become law in 1926 but for the action taken by the upper house, then made up in its majority by members who supported the party now constituting the government of the day. It is significant, too, that while the opposition in parliament at that time, headed by the Right Hon. Mr. Arthur Meighen, supported the program for old age pensions introduced by the Mackenzie King government, some very strong speeches were made by the opposition in the house at that time against the introduction of this measure. For instance, if hon. members will refer to Hansard of April 15, 1926, volume III, at page 2470, they will find, among others, this kind of expression, the view expressed by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St.George, a distinguished member of the Conservative party, who said:
Mr. Chairman, I am altogether opposed to the scheme of old age pensions as placed before the house in this resolution. I can understand an old age pension scheme which depends upon the incapacity of the recipient to earn a living, but unlike every other old age pension scheme with which I have been able to come in contact during a rather extensive search, this scheme altogether eliminates the element of incapacity. It assumes that at 70 years of age every Canadian who has lived in this country for 20 years is utterly incapacitated to earn a living. I object to that assumption, because actual incapacity should be the fundamental principle embodied in any pension scheme.
As the house knows, the act upon which this amendment is based provides for a pension as of right to every person in Canada 70 years of age and over, and the question of incapacity was dealt with by the previous administration through another legislative enactment. What was the view of the leader of the opposition? At that time Mr. Meighen supported, by the speech he made the same day, the position taken by Mr. Cahan.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: What has that to do with us?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext:
It has everything. It shows that this measure was first introduced by the Liberal party and it was opposed by members of the Conservative party. It is well for us to realize that and to keep emphasizing that what is now being done is by way of amendment to an act introduced in this parliament by the

administration of the right hon. gentleman who is now the Leader of the Opposition.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: Are you in favour of the amendment?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext:
What are the facts with respect to the act upon which this amendment is based? It will be remembered that in 1950 the government of the day proposed that an all-party committee should be set up to consider ways and means of improving existing old age pension legislation in this country. That committee had in its membership the present Minister of Finance as the main spokeman for hon. gentlemen sitting opposite. As a result of the deliberations of that committee certain recommendations were made to this house, and the government of the day accepted most of those recommendations.
The result was the establishment in this country of the universal old age pension system which provided as a matter of right to every citizen in Canada 70 years of age and over a pension based in part upon the principle of contribution-based, I say, in part on the principle of contribution. The significant thing is that it was, and continues to be, the only old age pension scheme to be found in any country of the world that does not have a means test.
This amendment, good as it is, must be related to the basic document of which it is a part, introduced by those representative of the party which sits to Mr. Speaker's left.
When the old age pension was provided for after the elections that were held in 1926, in revolt against the stand taken by a Conservative Senate, every citizen in Canada 70 years of age and over, on a means test basis, was provided with a pension of $20 a month, the federal government sharing the cost of this scheme with the provinces on a basis that was maintained until 1932. Now, hon. gentlemen opposite who bring forward this measure pursuant to election promises-and I commend them for that- are for the first time giving evidence of their official interest in this kind of matter, having denied themselves the opportunity during the dark days of 1930 to 1935 of doing something for the old people of this country.
Not only did we bring in old age pensions, those of us who support the Liberal party, but during the period from 1926 to 1930 we made some improvements in the legislation and from 1935 to 1940 income ceilings were raised. As minister of national health and welfare I had the great honour on two occasions of bringing in on behalf of the government, supported by those who sat behind us

when we sat at Mr. Speaker's right, increases in the basic amounts of the pension, with the result that we were able to say in 1951 that we had provided for the people of Canada the most comprehensive and, in dollar terms, the most generous old age pension scheme available to any people in any section of the world. It is with the background of this history that this amendment is introduced today.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: Don't forget the $6 a month you brought in.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: My hon. friend says, "Don't forget the $6 a month". I am coming to that. Let my hon. friend not forget that the only contributions his party made to old age security in this country is this. Out of the proposed $55 pension it is responsible only for the recommendation of $9.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: We have had to kick you all along.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: Last night the Minister of National Health and Welfare said this scheme would cost around $90 million.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: I said $96 million.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: Knowing something of the facilities that my hon. friend has for accurate calculation I accept, of course, his estimate of the total cost. The total cost of the amendment should be considered in the light of the total cost of old age security itself. As introduced in 1926 I think the projected cost was something in the neighbourhood of $12 million. When we embarked upon the universal scheme in 1952 the total cost of old age pensions chargeable to the government of Canada was in the neighbourhood of $90 million. When we left the benches now occupied by the hon. gentlemen the government of that day had introduced legislation which resulted in an expenditure of some $460 million by way of assistance to the old people of our country.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: Tell us about the $6.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext:
Now my friend is recommending an amendment involving an expenditure of $90 million. I commend him for that. Any assistance we can give to those classes in our country who need assistance will be approved, politics notwithstanding, by everyone in all sections of this house and in most sections of this country. It is important to realize the extent to which my friend now proposes to go. He is proposing an expenditure of some $90 million-an expenditure which some of the newspapers supporting my hon. friend are criticizing already as being an extravagant proposal-and that should be
Old Age Security Act
compared with the expenditure which we made in the last session to the extent of $60 million in addition to a total of $400 million for which the government of Canada had already committed the people before this government came into power.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: Yes; 22 years and 4 months respectively.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext:
My hon. friend says 22 years and 4 months. My hon. friend may sit there doing all the musing he wants, but the history of this legislation shows that it was a Liberal government that was largely responsible for its implementation. No last minute repentance on the part of those who opposed social security measures will alter this fact.
My hon. friend has made an important proposal in his amendment when he suggests that we should reduce the qualifying period of residence from 20 to 10 years. My hon. friend will, of course, have access to the departmental records. He will know something of the discussions that prevailed in connection with that matter between myself, as minister of national health and welfare, and the provinces. My hon. friend will have access now to other memoranda in the department which clearly indicate what was in contemplation in this regard.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: And your opposition to the idea.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: My hon. friend, the Minister of Trade and Commerce should realize that with his journeys to England, his sale of wheat and his problems in China, it would be better if he confined himself to those absorbing problems.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: The hon. member had problems in January; he is thinking of January.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext:
In 1951 the parliamentary committee gave consideration to the question of residence. If the hon. gentleman will look at the report of the committee on old age security he will find at page 111, paragraph numbered 69, the following expression of view, which was not the expression of view of one party but was the considered recommendation of all parties and unanimously given:
In the committee's view, it is not unreasonable to suggest that for the universal pension program a residence requirement of 20 years should be established similar to that which exists now under the present federal-provincial old age assistance program.
Now, what does this mean? It means that the Minister of Finance and the late hon. member for Lanark, for whom we all have the deepest respect and happy memory, shared

Old Age Security Act
the view of members of the C.C.F. and of the Social Credit party and of the party of which I am a member, that the period of residence for qualifying purposes should be 20 years.
Then it is significant that in paragraph 70 it is said:
With respect to an old age assistance program for persons 65 years of age and over on the basis of an eligibility test, it is the committee's view that a requirement of 15 years' residence should be considered.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: Why wasn't it?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext:
I am going to
give you the answer now. If my hon. friend will read Hansard he will find why. It was because the provinces, which had shared in the costs of old age assistance from 65 to 70, were reluctant to make any changes whatever in the matter of the qualifying period of residence, and among those provinces was Ontario. This is a matter of record. I am happy, as we all are now, that provincial-dominion relations are such that my hon. friends are now able to take a step which will have, at least in so far as other legislation is concerned, an exemplary effect in being able to persuade the provinces that they should reduce their qualifying period of residence as well.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext:
The only thing that was
wrong with the hon. member was that he could not persuade them.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext:
My hon. friend
is quite right; I was not able to persuade certain governments, including the government of Ontario, of the desirability of doing that very thing. But if I had, my hon. friend may be sure that I would have taken the step to bring about a reduction in the residential requirement under the existing act. I hope the country will now have the advantage of the close collaboration that exists between the federal government on the one hand and the provincial governments on the other, so many of whom share the same political convictions as hon. gentlemen opposite.
This brings me to the very important role of the provinces in this matter. Last night my hon. friend properly said in his speech, as reported at page 385 of Hansard for October 24, 1957:
We do not say that it is the final or perfect solution, or that there is any magic rightness about this particular amount. We make no extravagant claims as to the generosity of the amount we are now proposing.
I understand what prompted my hon. friend to make that remark, and he is quite right. No grant of any social benefit provided by this or any other legislation can possibly, in every instance, fully satisfy the existing need in the case of many old people. I agree with

my hon. friend. But there are many thousands of people in this country who are not going to fully benefit from the proposal made by my hon. friend or from the proposal which we made before June 10. There is only one satisfactory way of meeting that, and that is by the provinces of our country recognizing that they too have a responsibility in this matter. I suggest to my friends, now that they are in office and now that the relationship between the Prime Minister of Canada and the premier of Ontario is of the most intimate kind, that it ought to be possible for the Prime Minister of Canada to do something I was not able to do; that is, convince the government of Ontario that it has a responsibility and that in needy cases it ought to provide supplementary benefits under a more generous arrangement than now exists. What is the situation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext:
The hon. member was not
able to convince the provinces.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext:
In the provinces
of British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan there are supplementary benefits paid to needy persons, in the case of British Columbia right across the board. But in the case of Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: And Manitoba.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: -and Manitoba, all except Newfoundland and the three western provinces I have mentioned, the provincial governments are not bearing their share of the cost of assisting the elderly people of this country. The total cost assumed by all 10 provinces in the matter of old age pensions, apart from supplementary payments, is about $35 million. The federal government is assuming responsibility for $460 million, and now the $90 million proposed by the Minister of National Health and Welfare.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: Under the old formula they were taking about 85 per cent of the taxes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext:
It is not too much to ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare, for whom I have the highest regard, to use his influence in trying to bring about an improvement in that respect, particularly in our own province where so many people reside.
During the election we were told that the government was going to give us much more than is now proposed. We were told by the Prime Minister, "Elect me. I will call parliament together in September and I will give you the most generous old age security system of any country in the world."

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: So he did.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext:
"We are going
to do something about what is being done in the United States." Then listen to this statement. The Prime Minister said:
. . . I'm not going to indulge in any auction block type of politics by promising the impossible. Some political parties are promising the impossible and they know that they will not have the responsibility of power.
Then he said this:
We believe the old age pension is inadequate. We intend, this September, to call together a parliament and there and then fix a fair and reasonable amount for the old age pensioner, indeed for the other pensioners, and also make provision for a formula whereby due allowance will be made in the future for the rising cost of living, providing that it continues.
That last proviso was an essential part of the program.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: That will be looked after.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: But this amendment says nothing about that. This amendment does not live up to the promise of the Prime Minister of having a provision in the law that the pension will go up or down depending on the cost of living.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: Give us time.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: Has the government abandoned this particular feature of its program, or does it intend to introduce legislation?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: Wait till he has had 22 years in office.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext:
If it does intend to introduce legislation should it not do so at this session, because the Prime Minister said they were going to do it in the month of September Then what about the proposal made frequently during the election by the Prime Minister and also by the Minister of Transport that we should embark upon a program of assistance such as is provided to old people in the United States? There they have a superannuation system under which contributions are provided by the employer and by the employee.
It is true that those superannuation benefits exceed the monetary return of our old age security plan. It is significant that in the United States plan there is no financial participation by the government of the United States or by the state governments in any particular. But are we going to have, that plan? The Prime Minister said it commended itself to him. Are we going to have it, or has he now come to the conclusion reached by the Minister of Finance when he was a member of the parliamentary committee in 1951, a committee that examined this problem, that the universal old age
Old Age Security Act
assistance system being proposed by the government of the day was preferable to the particular superannuation scheme which I have just mentioned, and which exists in the United States?
Has he now concluded that our system is better? Has the minister come to the conclusion that our universal old age assistance scheme is preferable because it does not only embrace those workers in factories who can be reached by the principle of deduction of contributions from pay cheques.
The fact is that the United States scheme, which I believe has a lot to commend it, is something we had been considering and something that can be adopted, because it does not involve any action by government at all. Nevertheless we must look at the realities of the situation, and realize that if we adopted the United States system, as the Prime Minister suggested during the course of his election he would, we would not be touching the bulk of the population of our country. We would not be touching the farmers. We would not be touching the fishermen. We would only be embracing those who can be reached by the mechanism of deducting contributions from pay cheques.
So it is one thing to say that our system falls short of that of the United States, and it is another thing to say that we can study that system and also that we can adopt it without violating the principle of our own universal system. But my hon. friend, in the introduction of the amendment now before the house, has done nothing whatsoever to realize the suggestions made by the Prime Minister about the validity of the United States scheme. He does not do any more than confirm by this amendment the validity of the act which we introduced in 1951.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: And you are going to vote for the amendment, too.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: I said I was going to vote for it, and I certainly am.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but I must advise him that his time has expired.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as I listened to the speech just delivered I had to try to determine whether there had been an election on June 10 last. To hear the former minister of national health and welfare upbraiding the present government for not doing anything seems very strange coming from his lips. I must confess that when the election results were announced on the evening of June 10 one of the thoughts that ran through my mind was just what sort of approach the Liberal party would take in the House

Old Age Security Act
of Commons with respect to legislation. I wondered at that time whether the former ministers would have the brass, after having sat on their haunches for 22 years, to emerge suddenly as champions of last action.
I am sure, Mr. Chairman, that we of the C.C.F. have always considered that the differences between Liberals and Conservatives are superficial. It is simply a question of which party happens to be in office and which party happens to be on the opposition side of the house. But it does seem passing strange that the man who could have done so much when he was minister has now suddenly realized the enormity of the problem facing our senior citizens. Yet at the same time I did not hear one single suggestion during his 30-minute speech as to what he thought should be the figure, as to what he thought should be done at the present time. He went back into history-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: Does my hon. friend want me to deal with that?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext:
On some other occasion. I had expected that the Liberal party would now reveal to us just what they think the pension rate ought to be. We know that earlier this year they had a decision to make. They had to decide how much the pension increase should be, and they decided on a figure of $6. I think the niggardliness of the increase was one of the most important contributing factors in the defeat of the former government. From press reports I have read in newspapers from one end of Canada to the other it was quite evident before the voters went to the polls on June 10 that the people of Canada were not satisfied with the $6 increase. The government had allowed the position of the old age pensioners to deteriorate year by year and only-I am using the former minister's expression-at the eleventh hour, a few months before the election, did they bring forward a $6 increase.
We know what happened. The former minister would be quite happy to forget what happened on June 10, and in an effort to forget is going back 20, 25 or 30 years into dim history. Well, of course I understand the desire of the Liberal party to retreat into the past, but I was intrigued by a statement which the hon. member for Essex East had to make regarding the proposal made by Mr. King in 1926 about the old age pension.
I think all hon. members are very aware of the situation which existed in this house at that time. While I could not find the quotation, I can recall reading a statement made by Mr. Bennett to Mr. King, when Mr. Bennett quite properly pointed out that he only brought in the old age pension when

he had a gun pointed at his head by the late Mr. J. S. Woodsworth, the founder of the C.C.F. party, who at that time was the member for Winnipeg North Centre.
The reason we got the old age pension in 1956 was that both the old parties lacked a clear majority in the House of Commons and Mr. Woodsworth, as we are all aware, approached the party leaders-Mr. Meighen of the Conservatives and Mr. King of the Liberals-to find out which party would give the most firm undertaking that the old age pension legislation would be brought down. Mr. Meighen's answer at that time was very unsatisfactory; Mr. King, being a very astute politician, replied in a more favourable manner. As a result of the strategic position held in the House of Commons by two labour members at that time, the people of Canada got the old age pension legislation.
Thus it seems rather strange now to hear Liberals claiming credit for bringing in the old age pension legislation in this country. If credit is to be given, then I think in all honesty and fairness the credit for the old age pension legislation should go squarely to the late Mr. Woodsworth and Mr. Heaps, the two labour members in this house.

speechtext:
The attitude of the C.C.F. toward the resolution now before the house was summed up in the amendment which we moved in connection with the reply to the speech from the throne. Of course we expressed our great interest and support of

the legislation forecast in the throne speech. We went on to urge the government to bring down this legislation at the earliest possible date. I was very disappointed that the Prime Minister did not see fit to keep one of his pledges prior to the election, that there would be a September session in order that the senior citizens might have obtained the benefits of this legislation at an earlier date. However, we are most anxious to facilitate the passage of this legislation, and we are very pleased that there has been this interruption in the debate on the address in order that the house might consider this matter with all dispatch.
We have established our position in this house over the years in unmistakably clear language. We in the C.C.F. have always maintained that the hallmark of a good society is the willingness of the society to take cognizance of the needs of those among us who through no fault of their own, either through age or infirmity, find it difficult to take care of themselves. Hence we have always believed that what we should have in this country is a comprehensive social welfare program that will provide for all our citizens a decent standard of living. Consequently for our senior citizens we have always thought that the old age pension should be based on the need to provide these people with an adequate standard of living.
We believe that the old age pension is not a question of charity; it is not a favour bestowed upon our senior citizens. It is a matter of right, a right of citizenship which over the years our senior citizens have made great sacrifices to earn. They have built this nation, and in their declining years have a right to expect from this society a decent standard of living. Indeed, I can wholeheartedly agree with the statement made by the Conservative party prior to the election in respect to the new national policy adopted by it and endorsed, of course, by its leader. I am going to put this on record, because it is something with which we in the C.C.F. find ourselves in complete agreement, and I suggest this a commitment made by the government to our senior citizens.
We condem the meagre and niggardly assistance given to old age pensioners which leaves them in a position worse off in purchasing power than they were in 1951 when $40 a month was first established. No government worthy of its responsibilities can justify this picayune increase made to the old age pensioners. The Conservative party proposes to set the amount at a figure high enough to meet the needs of our older citizens.
I think we are in complete agreement with that. That same statement could have been made by the hon. member for Winnipeg

North Centre or the hon. member for Mackenzie or the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. We agree that the figure established should be set at such a level as to provide to our senior citizens a decent standard of living. Now, then, what is the figure?

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before lunch I had been discussing the commitment made by the present Prime Minister and his party to the Canadian public prior to June 10, and I had placed on record an excerpt from the new national policy under which the Conservative party had pledged itself to support the setting of the old age pension figure high enough to meet the needs of our older citizens. I suggest that the words "high enough" and the words "to meet the needs" are the most significant portions of that statement.
The question we must ask ourselves now is whether or not the present proposed increased rate does, in fact, meet the needs of our senior citizens. I do not believe that hon. members of this house would find it possible to live on $55 a month; much less, of course, would they be able to live on the smaller figure granted under the Liberal administration. But if we do believe that $55 a month will satisfy the needs of our senior citizens, then I suppose we can conclude that this preelection commitment has been met at this time.
While we are very pleased that the increase is coming forward, we in this party must remind the government that we must move forward until we reach the stage when the old age pension is high enough-in the words of the Conservative statement-to meet the needs of the senior citizens adequately. We in the C.C.F. party have pointed out that in order to provide a minimum standard of living an old age pensioner requires approximately $75 a month, and hon. members may recall that earlier this year, during the last session of the previous parliament, my colleague the hon. member for Nanaimo moved an amendment asking the government to increase the pension rate to $75 a month. The present Prime Minister voted against that amendment and indicated that the amount was too high.
I suggest that if we want to arrive at a figure based on economic reality we must

Old Age Security Act
take into account Canada's gross national product and satisfy ourselves that our senior citizens are getting their fair share of Canada's productivity. They would not be getting any special consideration, merely what they as citizens have the right to expect. Their just share of the national income would call for a pension of approximately $75 a month.
If hon. members feel that that figure is still too high, I would draw their attention to reports which have been made by various social welfare agencies in different parts of Canada. In one report dated August 1956 the Montreal social council agencies noted- and I shall quote the relative sentence- that an old age pensioner requires at least $70.87 a month in order to buy food and clothing, and shelter himself at current Montreal prices. That was in August 1956. Since that time the cost of living has increased, with the result that today the figure which we suggested last year of $75 a month is in line with the economic necessity of the moment. I suggest that if we are going to meet the objective of providing a pension high enough to fulfil the legitimate requirements of our senior citizens the amount this party suggested, namely $75, is the minimum which should be granted.
That was the attitude we took last session. I believe our position was valid then and, in view of the continuing increase in the cost of living, it is even more valid today. However, as I mentioned before lunch, the failure of the past government to recognize the needs of our senior citizens was one of the contributing factors in the defeat of that government. The $6 increase they brought forth did not meet with general approval throughout the country, and it appeared quite obvious that the new government was in a position where it would find itself in very difficult circumstances indeed if it did not proceed to grant an increase, and an increase which would have to be larger than the increase of $6 given by the previous government. Thus one may conclude that the figure of $55 contained in this amendment constitutes the minimum figure which could be arrived at by the government without running into serious opposition and criticism such as was encountered by the previous administration.
I am satisfied that the old age pensioners in my constituency were concerned about one thing, the amount of the increase. They knew that the political situation in this country indicated that some increase would be forthcoming, and the question they were asking was: what is the new pension going to be? Is it going to be $60? Is it going to

be more, or less? I think the old age pensioners of this country had every reason to expect that the pension would be set at a figure of at least $60 a month.
During the last session the present Prime Minister voted against an amendment calling on the government to increase the pension to $75. He indicated that while he was opposed to the figure of $75, by implication, at least, he suggested that $60 might be a reasonable figure.

I recall that at the time the then leader of the opposition suggested that the premier of Saskatchewan thought $60 would be a fair pension, and he endorsed the attitude of the premier at that time, so by implication he placed himself on record as supporting the idea of a $60 pension.
In any event, I suggest, while supporting this legislation, that we should bear in mind that there is a great deal more to be done and that this is only one step toward the kind of pension which we believe the senior citizens of this country deserve. Some people have told me that to them the $60 pension seems to represent a big increase. If this is so, if the increase seems to be large, it is because in former times our senior citizens have been so much neglected that they have been allowed to fall ever further behind year by year, to the extent that it required, not only one or two steps to bring them into line again with the others but several giant strides. However, I do not feel that because these pensioners have been neglected for so long by the former administration there is any excuse for not looking at the situation realistically now and setting the pension at a figure commensurate with the needs of those who will receive it.
Mr. Chairman, there are a number of other provisions in the resolution before the house. We welcome the proposed reduction in the residence qualification, but I suggest that the pension ought to be a right of citizenship and that the government might explore the possibility of lowering the residence qualification as suggested, I believe, by one of its own supporters the other day.
While the other recommendation with respect to increasing from three to six months the period of permissible absence from Canada seems to be a step in the right direction we feel nevertheless there is no justifiable reason for restricting the movement of our senior citizens. Today the old age pension is on a contributory basis. Every taxpayer in Canada through the payment of income tax and sales tax on his purchases contributes to his old age security. Why

then should the government say, "You will not have the right to go and live with your relatives in Utah, in the United Kingdom or in some other part of the world". Our senior citizens have earned their pensions and when in receipt of them they should be perfectly free to live anywhere they want to live. The proposed restriction of six months works a hardship on the people in the low income brackets. Those with means can leave the country in the winter months and return to Canada in order to protect their rights under the act whereas those who are not well off cannot do so. I believe the only fair way to deal with the situation would be to completely remove any restriction with respect to pensioners who desire to reside outside the borders of Canada when they qualify for pensions.
The proposed legislation before us today is regarded by those in the C.C.F. party as a step forward toward the goal which we in this group envisage. I mentioned earlier the work of the late Mr. J. S. Woodsworth in bringing legislation of this kind into this chamber in the first place. Since that time C.C.F. members both in the house and outside of it have fought to bring about a fair deal for our senior citizens. We are very pleased that there has been some recognition of the need for further increases but we call on the government to move forward in future sessions towards raising old age pensions to a level which in the words of the Prime Minister in the statement of policy issued by his party, "ought to be high enough to take care of their needs".
Is he convinced that $55 is sufficient to take care of the needs of senior citizens in providing housing, food and clothing for them? That is a matter of opinion; but I suggest we have a long way to go yet. We ought to move forward from the present legislation to the desirable goal of providing our senior citizens with the standard of living which they have every right to expect. In the meantime we in this group are happy that the present legislation constitutes a step forward toward the goal of this party of having a social security program that will guarantee to all Canadians who are unable to take care of themselves the type of standard of living which every Canadian citizen ought to enjoy.

Mr. Chairman, unfortunately many hon. members of this house have had to listen once again while other hon. members went back 31 years through history in an attempt to convey the impression that one political party or another deserves more credit than the rest for the fact that we have old age pensions in Canada today.
Old Age Security Act
While the hon. member for Essex East was speaking and during the earlier remarks of the hon. member for Regina I could not help but think; does the Canadian pioneer citizen, or any Canadian in fact, give one hoot in hades as to what happened in 1926?
It is probably true as was stated, that in 1926 some of the Conservatives-or all of them perhaps-may have opposed pensions. It may also be true that the then prime minister of Canada with gun at head introduced pension legislation in 1926. Again it may also be true that Mr. Woodsworth and Mr. Heaps, not by argument but by political pistols held at head, played some part in causing a Liberal government to introduce that legislation. Regardless of what may have occurred in 1926, Mr. Chairman, it is a known fact that all parties in this country today are in favour of old age pensions of one kind or another.
We may disagree as far as the amount to be paid or the regulations under which it will be administered are concerned, but surely no one should have thought that by reference to history he could prove any party opposes it today or that one party deserves special credit because it exists. The behaviour I have described reminds me somewhat of the idea held by some people that if eight or ten members of a party speak on a certain issue and only one or two in another party speak on the same issue the party having eight speakers favours a certain proposition more strongly than does the other. That fantastic sort of notion is held by some people.
Prior to June 10 the Liberal government in its attitude toward pensions believed that in the light of all known facts, including other commitments, we should increase old age security by an amount of approximately 20 cents a day. It was also believed by the government that we should increase old age assistance payments by 20 cents a day, 10 cents of which the federal government would pay. This was their belief, their conviction. Obviously it did not meet the approval of a great many Canadian people.
With reference to the Liberal administration I might point out that quite apart from the amount paid to our senior citizens the attitude of the former minister of national health and welfare itself probably had as much to do with annoying Canadians in this matter as anything else I know because he had a habit of standing in the house and claiming for his government, if not for his party, all the credit for everything that had been done in the field of old age pensions.
I recall that on January 29 last in answer to a question in this house he quite brazenly

Old Age Security Act
rose to his feet and claimed all the credit for, as he put it, his side of the house. You can well imagine how the citizens of British Columbia felt, how the people of Alberta felt and how the people of Saskatchewan felt upon reading that declaration by the then minister. His was the bad habit of claiming credit where he had no right to claim credit.
The Conservative government has now come to the conclusion that our senior citizens require an additional 30 cents a day, or approximately that sum. As far as those over 70 years of age are concerned, the federal government will pay the 30 cents per day. With regard to old age assistance the federal government will pay 15 cents and the provinces will pay 15 cents. Certainly I wish to express my deep appreciation of the fact that there has been an increase but I am not going so far as to agree that it is sufficient to provide a decent standard of living for our pioneer citizens who are dependent upon the receipt of their pension and that alone in order to meet the day to day cost of living.
It is definitely an improvement. I recall that when I first came to this House of Commons some 18 years ago our old age pensioners were receiving $20 a month. It did jump to $40; it did jump to $46; and now the proposal is to pay $55 a month. I have seen their status steadily improve, and I was pleased to note that the Minister of National Health and Welfare indicated that this was not intended as a final goal or the end-all as far as the amount of payment was concerned. I wish to express appreciation-and I know our old age pensioners will express appreciation-for that additional 30 cents a day. Let me also say, though, in connection with my observations that I do not feel it will enable those who are wholly dependent upon pensions to meet the cost of living, and that I also do not believe it is all that Canada can afford.
We talk of surpluses that worry us, surpluses of foodstuffs and surpluses of farm production. Our pensioners claim nothing more and deserve nothing more than a claim upon, as someone said, a fair share of that which is bothering us so much in this country, namely, so-called surplus foods.
The federal government has proposed that the period of residence for the purpose of qualification under the act shall be reduced from 20 years to 10 years. There may be some differences of opinion with respect to that action. I say the strongest argument probably in support of it is that it brings it into line with our Disabled Persons Act and our Blind Persons Act. The discrimination which existed heretofore certainly could

not be justified. Personally, I am very much in favour of that period of required residence being reduced from 20 years to 10 years.
The government proposes to double the period of permissible absence from Canada. I have knowledge of quite a number of cases, Mr. Chairman, where persons, because of health conditions and for no other reason, were obliged to leave our country for a period exceeding three months, more particularly during the winter time. And it does seem to me to be somewhat of a tragedy that those pensioners should encounter difficulties with pension boards because of the fact that they had been absent for more than the prescribed period of time. I think that change is most acceptable.
It is an important step forward, as are the proposed increases in the total allowable income, inclusive of pension. But I still cannot understand, Mr. Chairman-and I hope the government will try to assist me in understanding-why the total allowable income, including pension, either in the case of a single person or a married person, should be less than the allowable basic deductions under our Income Tax Act, namely $1,000 and $2,000. I hope the minister will try to indicate why he did not see fit to provide those basic exemptions when so many of his associates, while members of the opposition, strongly advocated such a proposition.
Now, Mr. Chairman, as I speak of this it reminds me of something else that I believe I should mention to the minister. Under our regulations today we find so often that where a person's income may exceed the total allowable income during a given year, even by as little as $10 or $20, he has been told that he must wait for a year in order to submit a second application. We accept the fact that he should be permitted to have, let us say, $1,320 but he has $1,400. I am using these figures at the moment only for illustration purposes. He has earned that $1,320 or has acquired it through earnings and pension during the past 12 months, and it can be assumed that the basic allowance was the amount required to keep him during those 12 months. But we say that because you had $80 more than the allowable you must wait another year before applying. To me that is a tragedy without reason and without excuse. Surely, it would not hurt us to say, You have $80 more than the maximum allowable; therefore, you should wait 70/1320 of the next year. I say, even if you were to say that, you would be assisting so many of those who have encountered difficulties as a consequence of that provision.

Let me say also with respect to the regulations, in the past the former minister of national health and welfare always tried to claim, or at least create the impression,-I will be fairer to him and put it in that way- that these regulations were drafted as a consequence of the representatives of the provinces and the officials of his department sitting down more or less from scratch and drawing the regulations. The fact, of course, always has been that the federal authorities have drafted the regulations and the provincial officials have been called in in order to come to some uniformity as far as interpretation and application are concerned.
I trust that the present government will go much farther in permitting the provincial representatives to assist in drafting the regulations with respect to the Old Age Assistance Act, which is the one I am speaking of specifically. After all, let us not forget that even though the former minister of national health and welfare tried to create the impression this morning that the bulk of the cost of the pensions is paid by the federal government, the fact is that in some provinces at least that certainly is not the fact and therefore the provinces should have just as much say as has the federal government.
In my own province of Alberta, for example, it is true that the federal government pays the total cost of old age security but I must remind hon. members here that a substantial part of the revenue of Canada comes out of my province, far more than is paid back into it, in spite of Liberal propaganda in the last election. Because of our vast resources, because of the wise policies administered in the development of those resources, quite a substantial part of the revenue of this country comes out of my province. My province pays half the old age security; my province pays the total cost of administration; my province pays a supplementary allowance of $15 a month plus, with very limited exceptions, medical, dental, optical, and hospital services to those pensioners and to the dependents of those pensioners. Therefore, I say to you, why should not the provinces be given just as much say in the drafting of old age security regulations as the federal government itself has to say in the drafting?
I do feel, regardless of what the Conservatives may have said during the election, that they would have been wise, had it been possible-I am suggesting that it is possible; I see no obstacle-to have placed in those pension acts an escalator clause, a provision under which those pensions would automatically increase with increases in the cost of living index.
Old Age Security Act
It would seem to me that the government could have escaped a lot of criticism; the house could have been saved a great deal of time and pensioners themselves could have benefited as the cost of living index rose. I think that was a provision that certainly should have been included in the legislation which is presently before us.
I am not going to occupy more of the time of the house, Mr. Chairman. We always supported the principle of old age pensions, whether it be old age security or old age assistance or whether it be other social benefits such as the disabled persons' pension and so on. We do not take a back seat to anyone in that respect, yet you never heard us claiming credit for all that has been done. I may even say in that connection that if people are going to start claiming the credit, they had better start in the provinces and not in Ottawa. They had better learn what the provinces themselves are doing to assist our pioneer citizens who are in receipt of pensions in one form or another. 1 say we do not take a back seat to anyone in this respect. We support and welcome the provision of these measures. We will probably be heard from again. The government will no doubt have us pressing them for a bit more realism so far as some of the provisions are concerned. But that does not mean for one moment that we are not grateful for those concessions that have been made. So far as I am concerned, Mr. Chairman, we have every justification for supporting them and we hope that the government will in every session of parliament which it might be fortunate enough to attend as the government go just as far as it has this time with respect to this matter.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with great attention to the intervention of the hon. Minister of Public Works and I am afraid he has his facts twisted. As a matter of fact I have learned, as it was easy to learn in the campaign in which I participated in my own province of Quebec, that it was the candidates, speakers and organizers of the friends of the minister-the members of the Union Nationale-who were threatening to cut the old age pension and family allowance payments and that in spite of the fact they were not made by the provincial government. We of the Liberal party certainly never used such threats or suggestions as a means of getting elected anywhere. As far as we are concerned we have been the victims of that kind of electioneering in the province of Quebec. We have been the victims of the strange bedfellows of those who sit on the opposite side of the house today.
Now, the Minister of Public Works has challenged us to explain the $6 increase for old age security, old age assistance, disability pensions, and other pensions which were increased in the spring. Well at that time, if I remember well, the then minister of finance, Mr. Harris, seemed to feel that we could devote the sum of approximately $100 million for increases in the overall field of social security apart from the increases in pensions and allowances for veterans.
It would have been easy for the government of the day to propose that the whole of this increase of $100 million or thereabouts should go for old age security, old age assistance, blind pensions and disability pensions but we thought there was another class of little people which deserved recognition and I hope that the Prime Minister, who according to the Minister of Public Works is so concerned about little people, will during the present session think of these really little people, those who are in receipt of family allowances.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext: That is the only election promise you fellows missed.

I will mention the election promises of the Solicitor General in a few moments. We thought that the amount available, according to the minister of finance, of about $100 million should be divided between the various classes of recipients of social security payments. The minister of finance at that time, Mr. Harris, had no doubt in mind the fact that the government would be

called upon to spend each year the sum of about $200 million as its share of hospital insurance. I hope the present government has also been thinking of that and it is going to go along with that proposal relating to hospital insurance. The total amount of increase which is proposed today is the same amount as was proposed in the spring by the last administration, approximately $100 million, but all of it goes to the one class of people and there is nothing for family allowances. Why is there nothing for family allowances? Is it that the Conservative party is still against family allowances as we have been led to believe for years and years in the past, and as we were told by a former leader of the opposition?
I was not surprised not to see in the speech from the throne any proposal for an increase in family allowances; I was not surprised that it was not mentioned by the Prime Minister who, according to the Minister of Public Works, is all for the little people; I was not surprised not to hear it mentioned by the Minister of National Health and Welfare; I was not surprised, in spite of the election promises of the Conservative candidates in Quebec and the speakers around them. Mr. Chairman, I am glad I have you drawing this matter to our attention, and I can assure you I will confine my remarks to the resolution before the committee.
I think it is obvious to the people of Canada that it is no longer necessary to have in office a government with an overwhelming majority. It is quite certain that if the previous administration had been returned with the sort of majority they had before, old age pensioners would still be compelled to look forward to receiving $46 a month; and I am sure hon. members opposite will not successfully appeal to the Canadian electors and be re-elected with an overwhelming majority such as the Liberals had.
In my opinion we are getting this sort of legislation because the government cannot forever overlook the needs of 800,000 of our citizens. I should say, Mr. Chairman, that Canada has a very interesting scale of pensions. Last year the minister of finance reported in answer to some of my questions that the highest pension available in Canada amounted to $1,041.66 a month. You had to be a retired judge to qualify for that. The highest paid in the Department of National Defence was $1,021 a month, and the highest by the R.C.M.P., $875. Superannuated civil servants can look forward to a maximum pension of $875. If one old Canadian needs $1,041.66 a month it is not easy for me to

Old Age Security Act
understand why the previous administration thought $46 a month was ample for another.
Before turning over the reins of office the previous administration did indicate that they were sorry for some of the people of Canada, and civil service salaries were increased in classifications of grade 6 from $5,460 to $6,300. That seems to be an increase of $75 a month. In grade 7 the increase was from $5,760 to $6,840, a difference of $90 a month. If you had the back luck to be getting a mere $7,000 a year, you received an increase of $1,300 or $100 a month plus a Christmas bonus of $100. I mention these things in passing, Mr. Chairman, to indicate that we did have money in Canada available for some projects. But in dealing with the old age pensioners the previous administration forfeited its right to govern because it stubbornly resisted meeting the responsibilities which they owed to this very large group.
Mr. Chairman, I received in the mail some time ago from an old age pensioner in Toronto, aged 74, a poem which calls attention somewhat graphically to the conditions in which some of these old people live. I spoke about this matter last session, but it was too late for anything further to be done. This is the poem-it is called "A Pensioner's Plea":
You may sing what a lovely day I would like to join if I may But first have mercy on poor me Raise my pension, set me free From the struggle, from the worry So I may live. Oh please do hurry Life that's shortened can't he sweet When our needs are not complete For, it's a pensioner I am And I'm really in a jam My rent nearly bleeds me dry And no matter how I try To live as God meant us to live That forty dollars just won't give Don't leave enough a dog to feed What sort of life must I then lead?
The rich get more, the poor get less Something our maker cannot bless So, gents of Queen's Park, have a heart Remember the poor, do your part.
This poem, "A Pensioner's Plea" was originally addressed to Queen's Park, Ontario but it was sent on to the House of Commons.
Mr. Chairman, I am sure the fact that so many people felt an increase from $40 to $46 was insufficient proved a major factor in turning out the previous administration. When the hon. member for Essex East was minister in charge of national health and welfare I drew to his attention an article called "Fourteen Days as an Old Age Pensioner", and I suggested that the former minister might be the leader of an all-party delegation which would try to live on a pension of that amount for a couple of weeks.

Now that the hon. member for Essex East has fewer responsibilities than he had previously, and since he could take part without worrying about any reduction in his salary, I suggest he might find it possible now to join such a delegation. I suggest that the new Minister of National Health and Welfare might try to get one member from his party, and perhaps the former minister of national health and welfare could, as I have proposed, represent the Liberal party. I myself would be glad to volunteer as a representative of the C.C.F., and I am sure the Social Credit group would wish to send a volunteer to try living on $55 a month in any Canadian city which the minister cares to designate.
Now I would like to call the attention of hon. members to an interesting article which was written by Mr. William MacEachern, one of the reporters on the staff of the Toronto Star in which he tells about his two weeks' existence with a one burner hot plate, a frying pan, a teapot, $20 and his own resourcefulness. He advertised in the Star for living accommodation and he received a number of replies. However, when he explained that he wanted the room for his grandfather, people opened up with a barrage of questions: "How old is he? Is he in good health? Does he drink? Does he still possess all his faculties? Does he have any chronic ailments?" The author goes on to tell his story, and I quote:
Then I asked my all-important question: "How much?". They quoted a price, usually $10 or over, and I explained, "Well my grandfather is an old-age pensioner, he gets $40 a month, and he is looking for a somewhat cheaper place. He couldn't afford much more than $5 a week." I could almost hear the ice crackling on the wires. Then the inevitable "Oh!", a few hastily muttered apologies, and the click of the receiver.
After two weeks, this young reporter's experience was over. He wrote in his paper:
I walked down the street, turned around at the corner and took a last look at my home for the past few weeks-a home with friendly hearts and cold rooms-a home that symbolized thousands of drab, cold rooms where our country's elder citizens wait for death, death the great repriever, not death the great leveller.
I had three cents in my pocket-the last of a $20 fortune. I tucked two of them away in a little compartment in my wallet-a reminder of 14 long, lonely days. I dropped the third penny into a weighing machine and watched the blurry figures whirl by-it stopped close to 157. When I started my life as an old age pensioner two weeks ago today I weighed 168.
Apparently, the readers of the Star were so interested in these articles that a great many of them wrote letters to the paper giving the author some hints on how he might have tackled the problem. One recommended, for example, that he should eat porridge for breakfast because it was cheap and filling; that he might economize by buying day-old

bread for 12 cents a loaf, and so on. Another chap suggested that he might get the young lads to catch sparrows for him; five sparrows could be bought for a cent, and if the authorities caught you you would not have to spend any of your pension for the next 30 days because during that time you would eat regularly in jail.
Well, the pension is to be increased to $55 and I am sure there is not a member in parliament who will vote against it. It is certain that $55 a month is a big improvement over $46 a month. I think we should not lose sight of the fact that while the Prime Minister was cautious he did give the impression that if he were Prime Minister he would not be satisfied with less than $60 a month.
While the hon. member for Regina City was speaking the Prime Minister suggested that he should quote the record which is exactly what I propose to do at this time. I have with me Hansard of March 28, 1957. When discussing the budget at that time the present Prime Minister, as reported at page 2774 of Hansard of that date, said:
As far as old age pensions are concerned, we believe the increase is totally inadequate for the needy; it is niggardly and paltry.
He was soon interrupted in his remarks but he continued to speak at some length. He was critical of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Nanaimo who had suggested that the pension should be increased by an amount commensurate with the increase in the gross national product since 1949, which would call for a pension of approximately $75 a month. At page 2781 of Hansard of that date the present Prime Minister is reported as saying:
I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks that the increase of $6 in old age pensions and the increases in blindness, disability and other pensions was simply a sop to political expediency ... I would be remiss if I were to hold out promises which could not and will not be met.
He made it perfectly clear he was not prepared to support the request for $75 a month but he referred to what has been done in Saskatchewan and mentioned that the Saskatchewan government saw fit to pay up to $60 a month for those in the 65 to 69 age group and gave the impression that because $60 was the maximum in Saskatchewan it would be a fair amount.
Later in the session on April 11 when the house was discussing the proposed increase in pensions I found myself facing a barrage of questions from the Conservatives who at that time were sitting on my right. When participating in the debate I referred to the fact that the present Prime Minister, then the hon. member for Prince Albert, said he could

not support our proposition. As reported at page 3444 of Hansard of that date I said:
The Conservative party has not said anything. There is an election coming on and no member of the Conservative party has set out that their program calls for $48, $49, $50 or $60, or what have you. No one has said this is what our program calls for.
Then an interjection occurred which is not attributed to an identified member. The name of the hon. member does not appear but it is my recollection that it was the present Minister of Finance who interrupted me and said:
Our leader said today $60-what are you talking about?
At any rate the interjection was contributed by a Conservative. I replied:
No, he said something like Saskatchewan.

It seems to me that while taking care of our older people, we should pay particular attention to the fathers of large families who have difficult problems to solve, problems which crop up from day to day, such as illness in the home.
Every day, or at least every week, people come to our offices to show us hospital bills running up into the hundreds of dollars, which they are in no position to pay because of their insufficient means.
