I am telling the hon. member that the gross national product in 1949, when the $40 pension was established, was $16.4 billion. Today it stands at $31.7 billion, which is an increase of nearly 84 per cent, if my calculations are correct. On that basis alone the figure we presented in this house earlier this year of $75 as a reasonable level for the old age pension would have been well justified, because on the basis of the proportion of the gross national product devoted to these social services the pension today should be $74.88.
There is, of course, another manner by which we might calculate the real value of the pension being paid. As I myself placed on record earlier this year, the $46 pension

which was brought in last session was actually only $37.18 in terms ol the 1949 dollar. Today it is rather less than that. Today, owing to the continual rise in the consumer price index, that pension amounts to $37.26 in terms of the 1949 dollar, and this new increase will, if my calculations are correct, bring it up to some $45 in terms of the 1949 dollar. So we are apparently going to give our old age pensioners some five real dollars more than they were getting when they were receiving a $40 pension.
It is suggested we cannot afford any more. So that we shall not be relying entirely on statistical evidence, I want to refer to a news item which appeared in the Ottawa Journal yesterday, datelined from Vancouver. This, I am sure, will be of great interest to the Conservative members of this house because it refers to a speech made by a Conservative member of the Ontario legislature in Vancouver, addressed to a number of fellow real estate operators. He advises the benighted inhabitants of British Columbia, to which province I belong, to focus their efforts on encouraging the immigration into British Columbia of the working classes because, as this gentleman said, there is no place there for a rich man to spend his money.
I am quoting that, Mr. Chairman, in order to prove that we apparently have in our midst a number of people who experience some difficulty in finding avenues of expenditure for their incomes. Speaking as a British Columbian, of course, I must confess to a certain sardonic and, perhaps, slightly snobbish amusement that a Toronto real estate operator should find the social and economic opportunities in British Columbia so limited. Admittedly there may be less opportunity in my province for the sort of vulgar ostentation which some people seem to regard as the outward mark of social fitness, although we do have a few millionaires ourselves. But I can assume that we have in this country now, by their own confession, people who may well feel that with their rather limited concept of the purpose of human life and in order to function properly in society they must find avenues for conspicuous spending. That being the case, Mr. Chairman, I think it is rather too early for us to suggest that the Canadian economy cannot afford the sort of pension which this group has been advocating over the past two years.
We are told, of course, that it is dangerous to increase it any further because of the danger of inflation. Unfortunately, the rug was pulled from under that argument by the man we hire to look after our money supply in Canada, the governor of the Bank of
Old Age Security Act
Canada, who earlier this year told us that the inflationary pressures, with which he was very much concerned, and about which I would remind the hon. Minister of Citizenship and Immigration the previous government did nothing, were caused by the vast, booming capital expenditures. He was even more specific when he pointed out that consumer spending, even those types of consumer spending which are based on a vast, inflated consumer credit, did not add materially to the inflationary pressures. So I suggest that the argument that we cannot afford to give more to the old age pensioners because of the danger of inflation has been exploded by the one person in Canada who has the best right to explode it.
There are, of course, many other drains on our economy which may make it difficult for us to provide older citizens with a more generous income. We have the drain of a continuing high level of corporation profits. We have-and this was brought very forcibly to our attention earlier this year-the scandalous situation in which there is no taxation whatever on capital gains of any consequence, as a result of which people are able to acquire fortunes without contributing to the economy from which those fortunes were drawn. We have expenditures on rather dubious measures of defence in this age of the sputnik which consume some 40 per cent of the revenues of this government, and we have not heard any suggestion from this government yet that they propose to consider these expenditures in a realistic manner in the light of the disturbing developments which have become evident in the last few months.
These are the places, Mr. Chairman, to which I suggest, if we really are concerned about our responsibility for senior citizens, we should turn for funds to provide an amelioration of their condition. In my part of the world, history tells us that the original British Columbians had a very brusque and efficient way of dealing with the problems of old age: they used to take their old people out to sea, put them on a rock at low tide to wait until the tide came in and thus solve the economic problem.
Perhaps there was a justification for it in a period in which the life of the tribe depended on every member of it being able to pull his or her weight but that is not the case in Canada today. We have actually and potentially a rich economy which can well afford to pay to the old people of this country something that will at least enable them to subsist on a reasonable basis.
I know the arguments, of course, that the old age pension is not intended to provide

Old Age Security Act
all the income of elderly people, that throughout their lives people should save enough to have at least a partial income at retiring age. Unfortunately for that argument statistics again show that the possibility of doing that is very limited. In fact, one of the ways in which the insurance companies in Canada sell their wares is to publish tables as to the fate of those who reach certain ages in our society and by that means they persuade a certain number of people to invest some of their funds in insurance policies. However, if one examines the report of the superintendent of insurance one finds the rather shocking fact that over $1 billion of life insurance lapsed last year presumably because the policyholders were unable to keep up their payments.
After all, Mr. Chairman, one does not need statistics to know perfectly well that the vast majority of people who reach the age of 70 have no savings on which to live and that whether we like it or not and however much it may outrage the exponents of initiative and thrift the fact remains that our economy is of such a nature that the greater proportion of our citizens are unable to provide for their declining years and you and I who are benefiting from the economy are the ones who should be deciding to make those declining years at least measurably comfortable.
Like the hon. member for Mackenzie River I am going to support this measure but I have a more logical reason for doing so. I think we can well afford it and I believe it is disgraceful that we are not doing more. I am quite sure that by the time the old age pensioners realize just what is the actual size of the $55 they are going to be given in terms of what it will buy in the market today, this government is then going to be faced with exactly the same demands as were made of the previous administration and they will come not only from old age pensioners.
The first time I realized the Liberal government was in serious trouble during the last election campaign was when I spoke at a construction job in my constituency. I had a number of friends working on that job, men with whom I had worked myself, and before I got up to speak one of the men told me, "I advise you to bear down heavily on the subject of old age pensions. The boys are burnt up about it". In the main these were young single men and when I discovered that this was their great bone of contention with the Liberal government I then realized that the Liberal party was in serious trouble. I suggest the Conservative party will find itself in serious difficulty also particularly if it takes no steps-and I am not in a position to say

what those steps should be-to curb and control the rapacity of landlords who rent accommodation to old age pensioners.
A day or so ago I received a letter from an old lady in Vancouver who told me that some of these landlords are certainly taking time by the forelock and the moment the word came out from Ottawa that the pension was going to be increased to $55 a month many of their tenants were informed that their rent would be increased as soon as their first cheque came in. These are the realities of this question of the old age pension.
I was glad to hear the minister say the other day that he was not pretending that this increase was anything in the nature of generosity on the part of the government. I have always maintained that no government is really generous whatever it does because it is not spending its own money and you can only be generous with your own funds. At that time he was basing the increase on the principle of justice but I suggest that in an economy such as ours virtually bursting with real and potential wealth, there is no justice in old men and women living in the rabbit warrens of brokendown houses in every large city of Canada existing on the old age pension as it is today or as it will be tomorrow when it reaches $55. There is no justice there and it constitutes a sore in the heart of our society from which we must all suffer.
I hope, therefore, that when or if our new government finally decides to bring down a budget in this house it will be one which in this connection will be based more firmly on the economic realities of Canada than is the present increase to $55 a month which, as I said, in terms of real dollars at the time when old age pensioners got $40 is only some $45.60.

Mr. Chairman, the debate thus far has demonstrated, I would say more than any other thing, that people in Canada have everything to gain from a minority government. At long last they are getting from the government the kind of legislation to which they have looked forward. The only thing that seems to have suffered, in my opinion, is parliament because we have been subjected to long harangues of political reasoning as to what somebody did in 1926, 1930, 1934 or 1944 or whatever the year might be.
It is not my intention to speak at too great length at this time but I would like to deal with a few points the minister mentioned when he introduced the resolution. As reported at page 385 of Hansard of October 24 the minister said:
The proposed changes are:
(1) an increase in the rate of benefit to $55 a month.

I am immediately caused to wonder just how the government arrived at the figure of $55 a month. The hon. member for Mackenzie River told us that Conservatives in his riding were advertising that the old age pension was going to be set at $76.50. I have no reason to disbelieve him but I would point out that in my own riding the Conservative candidate indicated it would be at least $60 a month. I cannot say how he arrived at that figure either. The hon. member for Mackenzie River also indicated that the C.C.F. party had advocated $75 a month and the fact is they brought in a resolution last year to that effect which I supported. He went on to say, however, that the Social Credit group had indicated in its brochure that it would pay $100 a month.
For the benefit of the committee and of Canadians generally I think we should keep some semblance of reasonableness with regard to this matter and with this in mind I propose to read from a Social Credit pamphlet entitled "It's Your Canada-The New National Policy With Social Credit". It contains a photograph of the Reverend A. B. Patterson and suggests that people might do well to vote for him which they did and we are extremely grateful to them for this. The fact is they did a fine job in supporting this party.

receive $100 a month. The pamphlet concludes by saying that this sum of $40 will be made up of equal contributions from Ottawa and the provinces.
The hon. member for Red Deer indicated earlier that his province of Alberta was paying $15 a month as a supplementary allowance to bring the pension in that province to $70. I am very happy to say that my own province is paying $20 a month in the form of a supplementary allowance, which will increase the pension to $75. I am quite satisfied that the government of my province will pass legislation which will ratify these changes and make any changes that may be necessary to bring the pension of those in need up to $75.
However, I come back to this same question. How did we arrive at those particular figures? Last session when we had our dear Liberal friends in the government seats on this side of the house they told us that all the country's economy could stand was a pension of $46 a month; that the total increase had to be $6. Despite all the increased unemployment that our friends cry about and that we know seems to be apparent we suddenly find ourselves in the position where this government is proposing to pay $55 a month. I am just wondering how these things can be done? I would not like to suggest for one moment, because I do not believe it, that we are not in a position to pay a higher pension than $55.
I notice the Minister of National Health and Welfare himself said at page 385 of Hansard:
We do not say that it is the final or perfect solution, or that there is any magic rightness about this particular amount.
I would agree with him, but I would suggest that possibly after we pass this bill and give the benefit of it to those who are to be the recipients of the money to be provided by it we should set up a committee in this house to discover exactly how far we can go in this and in other fields of social legislation so that we do not go back to the people as political parties and pretend that we can pay a sum which is out of keeping with the prosperity and ability of the nation as a whole. Certainly it is high time that we took the lives of people out of politics and came back to an actuarial basis and tried to have some reasonableness, some common-sense basis for what we are paying.
I think we can do much better than $55 a month, but that is not going to stop me from voting for this resolution and the bill because I consider that $55 is better than $46.

Old Age Security Act
The second point raised in the minister's speech was the reduction in the basic residence requirement from 20 years to 10 years. I would take no exception to that; I would agree that that part of the legislation is probably well advised.
Third, and equally important, is the extension from three months to six months in the length of time which the pensioners are free to spend outside of Canada in any calendar year without losing their pensions. The hon. member for Vancouver East told the committee that he had received considerable correspondence in respect of the possibility of people getting their pensions outside of Canada, not just for three months or six months but for the full year. They consider it is their right and they should have the right to collect what they have paid in, or more than that, because this is after all an insurance fund that they have paid into. Some of us may feel that we shall never collect it; others of us are more hopeful. There are some in the committee who receive it as of right. I take issue with the thought that we should make it available only to those who reside within Canada for a period of six months. In effect, all we are telling these people is that if you are wealthy enough to travel to Arizona or California from New Westminster or Vancouver in British Columbia, or from any other province, for that matter, you can stay there for six months and enjoy the benefits of this increased old age pension, but if you are not wealthy enough you will have to stay right where you are, stay put, because we cannot afford to give you that $55 in a foreign land for a full year.
I maintain, and I think the reasoning is sound, that since these people have contributed, since many of the members in this house, I am sure all, have contributed in one way or another, we would wish-certainly I would wish-that the minister could see fit to change the six months to the period of one year. It may be that when he answers later he can tell us how he arrived at the figure of six months. Our dear old Liberal government, the one which is past and gone and which seems doomed to unhappier days, if I interpret press reports correctly and would-be prognosticators of the fate of parties, thought that three months was the limit. It would appear that the minister might be well advised to tell the committee how he arrived at the figure of six months as compared with the three months that the former government had permitted.
I have only one other point which will take just one moment. The hon. member for Red Deer raised a question as to the figure


of $960 being used as the ceiling on allowable earnings plus the pension. I, too, would ask the same question. How did the government arrive at $960? Certainly it would seem not at all unreasonable to me, though perhaps I do not understand these things as well as some hon. members, that the figure should be $1,000. Why is it not $1,000, which is the income tax exemption for a single person? It does seem to me that if we can make it $960 we should be able to make it $1,000.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 10, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act to provide for jurisdiction in the handling of flax and rye.

He said: Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of satisfaction I have the pleasure of placing before this house Bill No. 10 for the consideration of hon. members. Those hon. members who were here last year will recall that I introduced a similar bill at that session. This bill is for the purpose of amending the Canadian Wheat Board Act and the explanatory note reads as follows:
The purpose of this bill is to bring flax and rye within the provisions of the Canadian Wheat Board Act and thus eliminate speculation with respect to these grains.
At the outset, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that this explanatory note in no way encompasses the full significance of this amendment to the Canadian Wheat Board Act. I have purposely drafted this amendment in such form that it will in no way interfere with the present Canadian Wheat Board Act except to introduce a new part V, the effect of which is to give further effect to part III and IV. This will mean placing flax and rye along with oats, wheat and barley under the jurisdiction of the Canadian wheat board.
Hon. members who are not familiar with the conditions of grain marketing in Canada will perhaps ask why it is that the western farmers are demanding the inclusion of more of their grains under the Canadian wheat board. At the outset I may say the reason is, first, that farmers generally in the prairie provinces are very happy with their experience in marketing grain through the Canadian wheat board. This amendment to the Canadian Wheat Board Act will, of course, in no way be a precedent and in no way a major deviation from the work of the Canadian wheat board in the past. As a matter of fact, during the period 1943-44 to 1946-47, the Canadian wheat board did in fact have flax under its jurisdiction. I might say that I am happy to have the honour and privilege of bringing this bill before the house because it does, in effect, bring before the members a move in the direction of orderly marketing which has been long sought by farm organizations.
I should like to give credit to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and its president, Mr. Herb Hannam, for the support given the principle which is now before us. In the presentation of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture to the cabinet in February, 1956, there is this:
As has been done in past years, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture would also request that flax and rye be marketed through the Canadian wheat board, so that these grains may benefit from the orderly marketing policies, and increase price stability that board marketing provides.
Canadian Wheat Board Act
This amendment, therefore, to the Canadian Wheat Board Act is favoured by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. I should like to give credit also to the Interprovincial Farm Union for favouring the principle that flax and rye should be included in the jurisdiction of the Canadian wheat board. I may say that this C.C.F. group is happy and proud now to have with us the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Schulz), who was formerly the president of the Interprovincial Farm Union. This organization has gone on record year after year in favour of the inclusion of these two grains in the marketing policies of the Canadian wheat board.
There is a very good reason why farmers generally favour the larger pooling of their grain for marketing purposes. The farmers have had a long struggle in trying to get some price stability and some orderly type of marketing. They have been subjected to vicious fluctuations in price over the years. Questions may be asked as to why farmers are in favour of this proposal. If hon. members will give some attention to the problems of the farmer, they will readily see that it is necessary to market grain through the specialized agencies in order to gain stability and control prices. Farmers generally do not want a feast or a famine. They have to cope with all the elements of weather, such as drought and hail. However, there is something that can be done for the farmer, aside from stabilized prices.
The farmers' problem in regard to these two great commodities is complicated on the open market. A year ago the federal government put flax under the jurisdiction of the Canadian wheat board. Speaking directly to this government I can say that probably so far as western Canada is concerned the result of the June 10 election and the defeat of many members of the Liberal party in western Canada was probably due to the fact that the government failed to have any close liaison with the thinking of farm organizations generally. I recall that when it was announced a year ago by the former minister of trade and commerce-for whom I have a great deal of respect but who I think had far too much work to handle to cope with it properly- that flax would be put under the jurisdiction of the board, I asked him if this was a deviation from former policy. He said no, that had been the practice just the crop year prior to that.
Of course, the following day he had to get up and announce that he had been wrong.
From that time onward, when flax was put under a quota and it was made impossible for farmers to decide on their own initiative when they should market their grain, the

Canadian Wheat Board Act farmers have been in the position that they are not able to market that grain except under a quota established by the Canadian wheat board. Of course, one other reason for the amendment being introduced at this time is the fact that over the past few years in western Canada congestion has made it impossible for the farmers to deliver flax and rye to the elevators at the time of their choice.
As I said earlier, the farmers want stability of prices and I should like to indicate to the house some of the price trends that have taken place. I have here a graph prepared by the Coarse Grains Quarterly, Sanford Evans grain trade year book, which indicates the average monthly prices of flax and rye for the crop year 1955-56. I should like to draw the attention of the house to the fact that while earlier the price of flax had been $3.40 a bushel it dropped to less than $3 by August; that it climbed to a high of about $4.15 in February and again dropped back in June to $3.40. Similar price fluctuations occurred in the case of rye. I would be very pleased, Mr. Speaker, if I could have the unanimous consent of the house to place this graph on the record because it does show in a much more graphic way than I can explain to the house the price trends for the crop year 1955-56.

Various arguments were put forward by the former government as to why it did not see fit to include flax and rye under the jurisdiction of the Canadian wheat board. I see the former minister of agriculture is in the house. Perhaps he will recall some of the arguments we had in this chamber when he was the minister and we in this group and other members were trying to get the inclusion of oats and barley under the jurisdiction of the wheat board. In the period from 1945 to 1948 different spokesmen for the government put forth various arguments why they would not and could not see fit to do so.


Finally, in 1949 or 1950 the house did pass enabling legislation and when similar legislation was passed by the provinces the Canadian wheat board was able to deal with these grains. I think the chief argument against the proposal during the period when we were struggling to get these two grains included was that oats and barley went into interprovincial trade and therefore were not commodities which could be included under federal control.
Further to my argument, Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out that the two commodities which I now urge the house to include under the jurisdiction of the wheat board are important for other reasons. The first is that on a relative basis exports of flax and rye have indeed been greater than exports of oats and barley in some years. I have here a table taken again from the Sanford Evans grain trade year book which gives the exports for the crop years from 1949-50 to 1955-56 inclusive.
I find that in the crop year 1949-50 exports of rye were 131 per cent of production and exports of flax for the same period were 148 per cent of production. In other words, there was a draw on existing stocks within the country. For the year 1955-56 the export percentage of rye was 97 per cent and the export percentage of flax was 55 per cent. If we compare oats and barley for the same crop periods we find that in 1949-50 the export percentage of barley was 14 per cent and that of oats only 6 per cent. Taking the crop year 1955-56 we find that the export percentage of barley was 26 per cent and that of oats 1 per cent. This does indicate that on a relative basis exports of flax and rye hold a very high importance.
To deal with income from these two farm products, I have here a table which should be of great interest to those wishing to ascertain the importance of this matter to our prairie farmers. This table is prepared by the dominion bureau of statistics and shows the cash income from coarse grains for the years 1949 to 1955 inclusive. In 1955 prairie farm income from the sale of rye was $6,325,000 while in 1952 it was $23,380,000. In the year 1955 the income from flax was $40,021,000 and in 1952 it was $29,912,000.
These figures show the comparative importance with oats and barley. It is a very short table but again, if I may, I should like to have the unanimous consent of the house to place it on Hansard. It shows, as I said, the income from the four grains I have mentioned for the years 1949 to 1955 inclusive. May I have the permission of the house?

Marketing of flax in 1955-56, Mr. Speaker, totalled 15J million bushels and it is significant that approximately 77 per cent of that amount was delivered between August and November, a four-month period. The price range during that four-month period was $3.02 to $3.25 a bushel. I should like to compare that with the price in March. All hon. members who are acquainted with conditions in western Canada will know that we often have very severe weather in that month and that it is impossible for the farmers to haul out their grain. With the price for flax at $4.16 a bushel which was the high during that period, only 400,000 bushels were delivered at that price.
I believe there perhaps should be more main reasons given in summarizing why the former government did not see fit to include flax and rye in the jurisdiction of the Canadian wheat board. I believe further that over the years the argument has been put forth in this house that it would overwork the officers of the Canadian wheat board and I have already indicated that the Canadian wheat board did in fact handle flax during the period 1942-1943 to 1946-1947. After that of course it was handled for a year by the Canadian wartime prices and trade board. Another reason why I think the former government did not see fit to bring these two products under the Canadian wheat board was that they wanted to leave the door open for speculation on these grains. In other words they wanted to leave the operation of the
Canadian Wheat Board Act Winnipeg grain exchange in such a way that the type of speculating to which I have referred could continue.
I do not want to dwell for a long time on this argument but I would like to say that the western farmers over the years have fought to stop speculation in their products and I hope every hon. member in this house will see fit to support me and those in this group in this move to bring under the control of orderly marketing, at long last, these other two farm commodities. I say this because I feel in doing so it will have the effect of stopping the speculation in the farmers' crops on the Winnipeg grain exchange and, in essence, will stop the gambling on farm products.
I think the former minister of trade and commerce has argued that these two crops, flax and rye, are after all small crops and therefore are insignificant and do not require the attention of the government in order to put them under an orderly marketing system. Well, I think my arguments this afternoon would indicate that such is not the case. Flax in particular has become a very important crop in western Canada and when you consider that the acreage of flax in that part of the country has risen from 1,030,000 acres in 1941 to 3,970,000 acres in 1956 you will very readily see the importance of this crop in western Canada.
I should like in my argument to put forward one other point in regard to price fluctuation. In 1948, as an example, when flax was under the control of the Canadian wheat board and a fixed amount was paid to the farmer as an additional participation payment, the farmers of western Canada received $5.50 a bushel for their flax in that crop year. Rye, which was left on the open market, for that crop year averaged $3.74J a bushel. However, by 1951 flax had remained at a relatively fair price contrasted with rye, which started to decline most disastrously and by 1954 was selling for 99 cents a bushel. Then last year, 1956, the average price of flax fell to $3.60 a bushel. Now I think it is only fair to the western farmer, who has gone along with the former government and to the two farm organizations which are attempting to get the ear of this new government, that we see some action in this important matter. While the former government seemed indifferent, not only to matters of this kind but to the cost-price squeeze facing farmers and so on, this new government we hope will see fit to meet the demands of organized agriculture. We hope they will also meet other demands coming from the representatives of the prairie farming area.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
I may say that I wrote to every municipality in the province of Saskatchewan and the replies I received to the question whether or not they were in favour of the inclusion of flax and rye under the jurisdiction of the Canadian wheat board were practically unanimous. In summing up my arguments I might say this:	the farmer wants, first,
orderly marketing of these two grains along with his other commodities; secondly, he wants stability of price which can be achieved through orderly marketing by the Canadian wheat board; thirdly, that these grains should be recognized as forming an important part of the export trade; and lastly of course- and this is extremely important-the farmers do not want speculation in their products. What they produce of course is after all the food of the world. I hope with that due consideration will be given to this proposal for a change in the Canadian Wheat Board Act and that I shall receive widespread support in the house in this respect.

wish to commend the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. McCullough) for again introducing this bill before the house, namely the bill to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act to make it possible for flax and rye to be marketed through that board.
We in this group for many years have argued that the marketing of flax and rye should be placed under the control of the Canadian wheat board. We have for years recognized the fine work which has been done by that board, working in the interests of those farmers of western Canada who produce wheat, oats, and barley. It is our feeling that farmers producing the other two major grains of the west, namely flax and rye, should be given the same consideration as those producing wheat, oats and barley. We have, as I pointed out, supported the Canadian wheat board down through the years, even though at times we have criticized the marketing policies which the Canadian wheat board has been forced to follow as a consequence, I might say, of the trade policies laid down by the former administration.
We sincerely hope the new administration will see fit to embark upon an entirely new trade policy as far as the marketing of our grains is concerned. The wheat board did away with the vicious fluctuation of prices which occurred for many years in connection with the marketing of our wheat, oats and barley. I can remember as a young lad, coming home from school, immediately getting onto a grain tank and hauling a load of grain to the town so that my dad would be able to receive the high prices for his wheat which were prevalent in the month

of September. We knew full well that unless he got that wheat on the market in September he would be forced to take a lower price in October or November. The Canadian wheat board ended that situation. Prices, as I have pointed out, have been stabilized as far as those three grains are concerned.
The hon. member for Moose Mountain has pointed out the terrific fluctuation of prices which occurred in the prices of flax and rye during the crop year 1955-56. He pointed out that the price of flax rose from a low of $2.97 to high of $4.16. The price received for rye varied from 87 cents to $1.30.
Mr. Speaker, I submit to you that it was not by accident that this low price for rye was reached in a period when it was impossible for the farmers of western Canada to deliver their grain. At the present time they often find it impossible to deliver their grain to the particular elevator they deal with, impossible because the elevator man is unable to accept flax and rye at that time. Farmers are not permitted daily freedom of decision in taking advantage of favourable market conditions.
Again, it has been suggested that farmers should stop growing wheat and grow other grain. If this suggestion is to be pursued it would mean that more and more farmers in western Canada would be turning their land over to flax and rye, and the need for a stabilized market would be further accentuated. As the hon. member for Moose Mountain has pointed out, farmers' organizations from western Canada have urged for years that the marketing of these two grain products, flax and rye, should be placed under the jurisdiction of the Canadian wheat board.
Representations were made to the previous administration on many occasions but seemed to fall on deaf ears. I know that representations were made to the new government on August 15 of this year, and I sincerely trust that our new government will see fit to support this particular bill which was so ably introduced by the hon. member for Moose Mountain.

Mr. Speaker, I know it is not usual for an hon. member who has made his maiden speech the day before to feel he should get up and make another speech the following day. However, as a farmer from the west, this problem vitally interests me as a person, and is certainly of great consequence to the people I represent.
Though I am only a new member of this house, I understand that this is a matter which has been debated in the course of a number of years during previous parliaments

and that it has, in a way, become more or less a perennial affair. This particular bill has been sponsored by the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. McCullough) on several previous occasions. At the time he last introduced it we had, of course, a different government and a different minister of trade and commerce. The position taken by the minister of trade and commerce and his colleagues at that time was that they would not have anything to do with putting rye and flax under the jurisdiction of the board, and since this attitude was not further discussed by other hon. members of his party I presume it could be taken as expressing the official position of the government of that day.
Now Mr. Speaker, in discussing this question with officials of the wheat board as I have done on several occasions, I found that during the period of congestion in the elevator system they have been reluctant to take on responsibility for handling any further grain, and it has apparently been their attitude that as long as this surplus position continues it would be wiser to leave the matter as it is today.
The Conservatives took the position three years ago at a conference in Saskatchewan of western members-this was an informal conference not involving party policy-that it would be better to leave flax on the open market as a barometer which would tell farmers whether the wheat board was doing a good job or not.
The farm organizations, though generally favourable to flax and rye being handled by the board were not completely in agreement. On the surface they were in agreement, but some of their officials were not completely in accord for the reason that in their opinion no further burden should be placed on the wheat board at this time of serious congestion. Such an attitude would be especially understandable now that the board is being asked to handle the cash advance. The farmers themselves are divided as to the feasibility of placing responsibility for flax and rye on the wheat board-but I believe the majority favour it.
My own opinion-and I am here to express my own opinion-and I think it is also the opinion of the people whom I represent, is that desirable as it may be to have these two grains under the control of the board it would be asking too much to instruct the board to undertake such a responsibility, having regard to the prodigious amount of detail which would be involved in this present crop year, especially, as I have previously pointed out, at a time when officials of the board would be reluctant under present circumstances to take on further obligations.
Canadian Wheat Board Act
I do not bring up these points with any purpose of placing anything in the way of this bill. If it can be shown to this house that it is practical this year, in the circumstances I have indicated, then I think we should give the matter further consideration. But these are some of the questions to which hon. members in this house have not had answers up to the present time. We have listened to a large number of statistics, read by the hon. member for Moose Mountain in very great detail. I am sure that to the majority of hon. members they did not convey too much meaning, taking them as he was giving them orally.
It could be that one way to resolve this issue would be for the committee on agriculture to hold hearings on it. Everyone concerned could then make a submission and, in consequence, the committee would perhaps be in a position to assess intelligently the issues involved and come back to the house with the proper answers. In other words, Mr. Speaker, what I have said is, briefly, this: desirable as it may be to have these grains under the control of the board when the board is functioning in normal conditions, I do not think we should ask these people to take on this extra burden now, especially as during the next few days, when the bill providing for cash advances is passed, they will be asked to handle a tremendous amount of detailed work in connection with that proposal since a very large percentage of the flax has been sold this year. I think we should give the board an opportunity to get this load of other grains off its back before we pile another on top of it. However, if that answer does not appeal to all hon. members-and I am sure it is reasonable- then I suggest that a committee of this house investigate every possibility before we make any rash moves.
I would conclude by expressing the hope that the committee will be in agreement with me that we can resolve this question, but should not do so in haste and as a result do something to injure the operations of the wheat board which I am sure the majority of the hon. members of this house would not wish to do.

Mr. Speaker, due to the fact that the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. McCullough) has so adequately and comprehensively laid this matter before the house it will not be necessary for me to go into any great detail. I am sure it is a matter of satisfaction to him and to those he represents that he has already been commended by hon. members on the other side of the house for having brought

Canadian Wheat Board Act this bill before it and given hon. members an opportunity to express in principle their opinion upon it.
Naturally we are most interested to hear the attitude of the government on this question and I assume that the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Muir) who was the first spokesman in his party to speak about it did so on behalf of his government. If that is so there is good room for hope that this bill is going to carry this day because the hon. member recommended-on behalf of the government no doubt-that the bill go to a committee.
Of course the only way this bill can go before a committee is to be adopted on second reading and then it can go to the committee for close study and be further considered as to detail and I believe that procedure is the one we should adopt. That would also meet the reservation expressed by the hon. member who preceded me in relation to the attitude of the wheat board itself because if this bill is now adopted in principle and sent to a committee the members of the wheat board or any other officials who are interested, including representatives of the farm organizations, could appear before that committee and state their opinions and offer suggestions as to the details of the bill.
I hope the vote on this bill will be favourable. I am sure that at least one member of the Progressive Conservative party must be thoroughly in support of this legislation. I refer to one of my colleagues from Manitoba, the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jorgenson). I say this because I have followed his career in the Manitoba farmers' union and know that he is one of the former officials of this organization who as a district director was responsible with other district directors in framing the resolutions which were contained in briefs presented to the former government and which in the near future will perhaps be presented to this government by the Manitoba farmers' union demanding that this type of legislation be placed before parliament.
In these circumstances I hope we will have the united support, as has already been indicated, of the Social Credit group and for which we are duly grateful and we will also expect the full support of the members supporting the government.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to represent a constituency which is largely urban. The constituency of Winnipeg South is situated rather close to the Winnipeg grain exchange and the wheat pool as my hon. friends in the far corner of the house realize. Notwithstanding the fact that it is largely urban and residential there is on the outer fringes
[Mr. ZaplitnyJ

the market gardener and farmer who have a small acreage. In certain instances these farmers may be producing flax and rye. Perhaps it is because of their close proximity to the wheat board and the grain exchange that I feel they could be delighted that they have one residual area of free enterprise in which they can operate.
In addition to that there is a sugar beet manufacturing industry in the Fort Garry portion of my constituency and in the area to the south of this municipality, a large number of farmers have prospered through this free enterprise.
It occurred to me-and it seems a reasonable and justifiable suggestion-that this sort of bill should be given full consideration by the committee on agriculture as was suggested by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Muir), particularly in view of the declared diversification of opinion I have brought to the attention of the house. In its sittings the committee could bring before it representatives of the farmers' unions which hon. members in the far corner of the house seem to represent more than they do the general populace of their constituencies.
Before coming to Ottawa I had the opportunity of sitting around the table with members of the Manitoba farm union and their primary concern was the cash position of the farmers which this government has already taken steps to improve. Throughout the course of the entire evening there was no suggestion on the part of those representatives that this sort of bill should be given consideration at an early date or at the initial sittings of this house.
I am reminded of a letter I received from one farmer which consisted of about 14 words in which he said, "While we were under the grain exchange for marketing purposes things were good and they ain't been since". I do not suggest for a moment to this house that I ally myself with the idea of recovering the operations of the Winnipeg grain exchange as they existed in years gone by but as yet I do not shut the door completely on the possibility of the grain exchange and the wheat board operating co-operatively side by side as a dual outlet for our grain.
This is something that I say with great sincerity because I do feel that under the free and open marketing of all grains there is a great possibility, indeed almost a probability, that we would not have the fantastic grain surplus that we have on our hands at the present time; but I wish to make it clear, and amply clear, that I would not subscribe to the operation of the Winnipeg grain exchange exclusively as far as grains are concerned.

The reasons already presented to this house are that the present wheat board is operating to full capacity in dealing with the tremendous surplus we have; that we are dealing indeed with legislation for cash advances, which we expect will shortly be passed in this house, and those reasons almost, I would suggest to the house, preclude the addition of the operation and control of these two crops of flax and rye. For that reason I think this bill is premature. It has not been considered by the government and cabinet; it has not been considered by the western members of the government in caucus; it has not been considered by the caucus of the government as a whole. The general feeling for the time being at least should be that these crops can be left on the free and open market as cash crops that are bringing reasonable returns to the farmer. Indeed, perhaps they are the only crops that are bringing such farmers any cash at all.
I know my hon. friends in the corner across the way would like to see everything brought under the control of government agencies and boards of one kind or another; but we who have seen the inspired and tremendously productive operation of free enterprise in the world of business recognize that the temporary crisis which have developed in the field of agriculture do require the intercession of government for the time being to endeavour as much as possible to put the farmer in a position where he has cash on hand to keep in line with his current expenses.
May I point out, Mr. Speaker that-I do not speak for the government any more than the hon. member for Lisgar does. We are speaking only for the reason that we have not considered this thing at all in cabinet or in caucus; we speak as individual members giving private opinions on such subjects. We favour government intercession only to the point where it rectifies a crisis such as exists at the present time among our farmers owing to the lack of cash. The government has taken steps along appropriate lines, favoured by all sides in this house, to correct that situation. I think that legislation will be introduced shortly and voted upon. If we take this one additional step at the present time to bring under the control of the wheat board flax and rye I do not think it will be long before the hon. gentleman in the far corner will be suggesting that turkeys, butter, eggs, sugar beets and sunflowers should all be brought under a similar type of board and controlled by the government.

I have been advocating that for years.
Canadian Wheat Board Act

The point my hon. friend forgets-and he knows why his numbers are not larger than they are-is that they have been advocating this sort of thing for years and there are still Canadian citizens who do not want the government to run their lives from morning until night.

I wonder whether the hon. member for Winnipeg South will permit a question. Can the hon. member say whether or not he has noticed that the farm organizations, including the wheat pools and the farmers' union, have asked that a measure like this be adopted?

I would be very happy to answer the hon. member. I have not personally, as I told him, been consulted about this and I have been consulted by a great number of other organizations on similar problems and by quite a few farm organizations on other problems. If the hon. member suggests, and probably he is right, that this is a very pressing problem that has been urgently submitted to members of his group, I can assure him that it has not been brought with anything like the same vigour to the attention of the private members who are not in the agricultural business and, as the hon. member knows, require to be educated on the needs of farmers.
We are never too ashamed to admit that we do not have the specialty that those of you who are farmers have. Those of you who are farmers know a lot about farming. I happen to be a lawyer and I think probably I know a lot more about law than the average farmer does. But I think I can say with humility, as one private member of the house, I want to hear from those organizations through their representatives on the agricultural committee; I want to know how desperate the need is and I want to have substantial proof that these two crops have not been returning the farmer more cash than anything else that he is dealing with on his farm. If I can be convinced, in the normal course of events, just as any other member of the government, that this is a very desperate need, then I assure my hon. friends across the way that the government will give the proper consideration to it and announce a policy in this house in due course.
I emphasize again that I oppose the creeping into every facet of our democratic life in Canada the agencies of government that will swell the civil service and add more fixed costs to the taxpayers of this country. This is something that my hon. friends over

Canadian Wheat Board Act there have advocated without success for years. I assure them that as long as I am in this house anything that smacks of that sort of thing will be responded to with a great deal of sincerity and honest opinion from my side of the house by more members than myself.
